Snowflake Foundations: Hands-On Lab

82 minutes of core exercisesHealthcare dataNo experience needed

The story

It's your first day as an analyst at a regional health network. Your manager hands you three files: patients, visits (we call them encounters), and doctors' notes. She wants to know where the money is going, and she'd like a simple app the care team can click around in. You've never used Snowflake. By the end of this lab, you'll have done all of it.

What you'll do

1. Find your way around

Tour Snowsight, the Snowflake web interface.

2. Meet CoCo

Try Cortex Code right inside Snowsight: ask questions in plain English.

3. Load data

Upload three CSV files into tables.

4. Ask questions with SQL

Filter, sort, total and join your data, then try some challenges on your own.

5. Undo a mistake

Use Time Travel to recover changed and deleted data.

6. Build an app

Make an interactive Streamlit app, using only Python.

7. Control access (optional)

Create a role for the care team and inspect its grants.
Your route through the labThe core exercises are estimated at 82 minutes, with login and account access confirmed beforehand. For a beginner-led session, allow 105-120 minutes for questions, startup waits, and troubleshooting. SQL Challenges and Roles and Access are optional extensions after Wrap-Up. Each module also has an always-visible Try it with CoCo practice section with a CoCo mascot heading. These are extra practice, not part of the core timing. Completing every optional activity requires additional time.
If your session is 90 minutesFollow the core modules through Wrap-Up. Keep the Meet CoCo introduction, but save the extra Try it with CoCo sections, SQL Challenges, Roles and Access, the bonus clone, and app deployment for later. If behind, defer the Query Profile tour. Do not skip row-count checks, creating the app's view, restoring the changed/dropped tables, or suspending compute at the end.
Your personal trial accountA personal Snowflake trial account will be provided to each participant. It remains active for three days after the lab, so you can revisit the exercises and try the optional activities. Use the access details supplied by the facilitator; there is no need to sign up for another account.

Before you start

  • Download lab data (ZIP) Unzip it on your laptop. It contains only patients.csv, encounters.csv, and clinical_notes.csv. Keep their names unchanged; later you will upload the three CSVs, not the ZIP.
  • A laptop with Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari. You don't need to install anything.
What comes next This lab is the "Day 0" warm-up for the Value-Based Care Cortex AI Lab. The hands-on tasks here prepare you for that lab.

Snowsight Tour & Workspace Creation

1. Sign in to your provided personal trial account

  1. Open the personal trial account URL supplied by your facilitator and follow the supplied sign-in instructions. This is your own lab account, available during the workshop and for three days afterward. Do not use a work or production account, and do not create another trial.
  2. Confirm the organization/account name in the account menu. If you see production data or do not recognize the account, stop and ask your facilitator.
  3. Bookmark the URL. Keep this guide and Snowsight in separate browser tabs so you can switch between instructions and your work.
  4. Set your role once: open your user menu (your name, usually lower left), choose Switch role → ACCOUNTADMIN, and leave it selected for the entire lab, including optional exercises. If it is unavailable, stop and ask your facilitator.
Workshop account onlyUsing ACCOUNTADMIN throughout is a shortcut for this isolated account with fictional data, not a production practice. In production, use task-specific, least-privilege roles. Do not run this lab in a work account.
Before the lab sessionThe facilitator should confirm login, ACCOUNTADMIN access and default-role configuration for new SQL sessions and CoCo, an available warehouse, and CoCo access. Account provisioning and AI enablement are prework, not timed exercises. All downloadable records are fictional teaching data, not real patients or a Synthea export.

Take a 5-minute tour

After you log in you're in Snowsight, the Snowflake web interface. Click through each item in the left menu:

Menu itemWhat it's forYou'll use it in

Can't find a menu item?Snowsight's menu changes from time to time. Use the search box at the top of the left menu, or look for your username in the bottom-left corner. Clicking it shows your current role; keep ACCOUNTADMIN selected for this lab.

2. Follow this tour, one stop at a time

  1. Catalog → Explorer (or Database Explorer). Expand a database, then a schema. Notice how tables and views sit inside schemas. You might see SNOWFLAKE; sample data is not required. An empty list can mean your role has no visible objects, not that the account is broken.
  2. Admin → Warehouses. Find an available warehouse. Read its name, size and state. Suspended is normal: an auto-resuming warehouse wakes up when needed. Do not resize or resume anything during the tour. We create LAB_WH later.
  3. Monitoring → Query History. Filter to your own user if available. This records executed statements, their status and timing; it is not where you edit SQL. An empty history is fine on a new account.
  4. Projects → Streamlit. Locate the deployed-app list, but do not create an app here. Later we create and preview our app inside the snowcamp workspace.
  5. Projects → Workspaces. This is your home base. Locate the file tree, editor tabs, SQL context selectors, Run control, and Results pane. Next, create a dedicated workspace rather than leaving lab files scattered in My Workspace.
Navigation variesIf Catalog uses the label Explorer, choose it. You can also browse databases inside Workspaces. If you cannot see Warehouses or Query History, ask the facilitator rather than changing account-wide permissions.

3. Connect your private snowcamp workspace to Git

First allow this lab account to read the public repository. This one-time bootstrap must happen before creating the Git workspace.

  1. In Projects → Workspaces → My Workspace, use + Add new → SQL File to create git_bootstrap.sql.
  2. In your provided lab account only, paste the following SQL and run the entire block. If ACCOUNTADMIN is unavailable, ask your facilitator to create the integration; do not request admin access to a production account.
USE ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

CREATE API INTEGRATION IF NOT EXISTS SNOWCAMP_GIT_INTEGRATION
  API_PROVIDER = git_https_api
  API_ALLOWED_PREFIXES = (
    'https://github.com/sfc-gh-gfuribondo/snowcamp-0day-lab'
  )
  ENABLED = TRUE;
  1. The Snowsight user-menu role should still be ACCOUNTADMIN, selected at sign-in. That role controls which integrations the creation dialog can see. The bootstrap sets the SQL session to the same role; later exercises contain no role-switch commands.
  2. Open the workspace selector/header and choose From Git repository. Do not choose Shared workspace.
  3. Paste the repository URL below. Set Workspace name to snowcamp, select API Integration SNOWCAMP_GIT_INTEGRATION, choose Public repository authentication, then select Create.
https://github.com/sfc-gh-gfuribondo/snowcamp-0day-lab.git
  1. Confirm snowcamp is selected and the branch is main. Expand data to find setup.sql and load_data.sql; expand streamlit to find streamlit_app.py.
  2. Find explore.sql and time_travel.ipynb at the workspace root. They already contain the SQL Basics and Time Travel exercises; do not create blank replacements. Open explore.sql to preview its numbered sections, but wait until after loading data to run them. Its SQL toolbar should show ACCOUNTADMIN; leave that role unchanged.
No GitHub sign-in requiredThe public-repository connection brings code into your private workspace; it cannot push your edits back to the lab repository. You do not need to commit or push during the lab. Download your edited files before your trial expires.

Meet CoCo: Your AI Assistant in Snowsight

Cortex Code (CoCo) is an AI assistant built into Snowsight. You can ask it questions in plain English and it can write SQL, explain results, suggest fixes, and help you learn.

Check access before the workshop Use your provided personal trial account. The facilitator should confirm the required database roles, AI feature access, cross-region inference, and non-zero daily credit limit before the lab. If CoCo is unavailable, ask the facilitator to check this account; do not create another trial or add payment details as a troubleshooting step. If unavailable, follow the copyable SQL examples and watch the facilitator demonstrate CoCo. See CoCo access requirements.

1. Open CoCo

  1. Look for the CoCo icon in the bottom-right corner of Snowsight.
  2. Click it to open the CoCo chat panel.
Why this matters You don't need to memorize SQL syntax. CoCo can write queries for you, explain what they do, and help when you get stuck. It's especially useful when you're learning, because you can ask "why" and get an answer in plain language.

2. Ask it something

Try typing one of these into the CoCo chat:

  • What databases exist in my account?
  • Explain the SQL for creating a warehouse called LAB_WH. Do not execute it.
  • What's the difference between a database and a schema?

CoCo can provide SQL, explanations, and suggested file edits. Review suggested changes before applying them. Copy generated SQL into your Workspace SQL file when you want to run it yourself.

3. Use it throughout the lab

Keep CoCo open alongside your Workspace as you work. Include relevant code, error messages, and fully qualified table names in your prompts:

When you're inTry asking CoCo
A SQL file (SQL Basics)Explain this query or Why am I getting this error?
The query profile (SQL Basics)Why is this query slow?
A Streamlit app (Streamlit)Add a pie chart showing cost by payer
AnywhereWrite a query that shows the top 10 patients by total cost
Good to know CoCo can execute multi-step tasks, not just suggest SQL. It starts with your default role, which the facilitator should configure as ACCOUNTADMIN in this workshop account. The user menu, SQL files, and CoCo have separate contexts; setting one is not a global role change. If any context shows a different role, stop and ask the facilitator to correct the initial setup rather than switching roles during the exercises. For this introduction, choose + → Restrict this chat → Read-only and ask for explanations or draft SQL. Review generated queries and suggested edits; AI output can be incorrect.

Try it with CoCo

Try one now; no loaded tables required.Keep the chat read-only. Open the named file when a prompt asks about it. If CoCo cannot see it, attach the file or select its text as context rather than accepting a guessed answer.

1. Get a map of your new workspace

I just connected the snowcamp lab repository. Inspect its file list, without running code or changing files. Give me a five-step route from setup to a working app, naming the files I will open. Explain why seeing patients.csv in this workspace does not mean PATIENTS is loaded. If you cannot see the files, tell me what context to attach. Keep it under 150 words.

Success check:Find the named files in your workspace and explain the separate stage-upload step.

2. Predict what setup will do

Open data/setup.sql first.

Read data/setup.sql without executing it. Explain which compute resource runs SQL and which runs the Python app. Identify the statements that change account or user defaults, and tell me what rerunning this script changes versus leaves alone. Does running it load any patients? End with one question for me to answer before I run setup.

Success check:Identify LAB_WH, LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL, the default-setting statements, and the fact that setup leaves the tables empty on a first run.

3. Solve a tiny healthcare puzzle

We have three fictional visits: patient P1 costs $100, patient P1 costs $200, and patient P2 costs $300. Ask me to predict the visit count, distinct patient count, total cost, and average cost per patient. Wait for my answer. Then explain it and draft one Snowflake SELECT using VALUES so I can try it without loading files or creating tables. Do not execute SQL or change anything.

Success check:Explain why three visits are not three patients. Review the generated SQL; running it yourself is optional and needs an available warehouse.

Set Up and Load Data

1. Run setup.sql in the snowcamp workspace

  1. Return to Projects → Workspaces → snowcamp. If missing, complete the required workspace creation step first.
  2. Open data/setup.sql in your Git-connected workspace. The Snowsight user menu and SQL toolbar should still show ACCOUNTADMIN. Leave the role unchanged.
  3. Use the dropdown next to Run → Run all. The script creates lab infrastructure, sets the account's default Streamlit compute pool to LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL, and sets your user's default warehouse to LAB_WH. It does not load data or erase existing rows. The same code is shown below.
  4. After it finishes, check the SQL toolbar: ACCOUNTADMIN · LAB_WH · DAY0_LAB · HEALTHCARE. Inspect the compute-pool result for LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL and the parameter result for the same default pool. The last result should list three tables.
Workshop account onlyThis setup changes an account-wide Streamlit default and your user's default warehouse. Run it only in your provided personal lab account. Rerunning reapplies those defaults; existing objects are not replaced. If any statement fails, stop and ask the facilitator rather than changing roles or bypassing account restrictions.
-- 1. A small compute engine that pauses itself after 60 idle seconds
CREATE WAREHOUSE IF NOT EXISTS LAB_WH
  WAREHOUSE_SIZE = 'XSMALL'
  AUTO_SUSPEND = 60
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE;

-- 2. Small CPU nodes for Streamlit; preview plus optional deployment
CREATE COMPUTE POOL IF NOT EXISTS LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL
  MIN_NODES = 1
  MAX_NODES = 2
  INSTANCE_FAMILY = CPU_X64_XS
  AUTO_RESUME = TRUE
  INITIALLY_SUSPENDED = TRUE
  AUTO_SUSPEND_SECS = 60;

-- Workshop account only: default pool for new Streamlit apps
ALTER ACCOUNT SET DEFAULT_STREAMLIT_COMPUTE_POOL = 'LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL';
-- With no user name, ALTER USER changes your own default warehouse
ALTER USER SET DEFAULT_WAREHOUSE = 'LAB_WH';

-- 3. A database and schema (the "folders")
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS DAY0_LAB;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE;

USE WAREHOUSE LAB_WH;
USE SCHEMA DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE;

-- 4. A database stage for files, plus a reusable CSV format
CREATE STAGE IF NOT EXISTS LAB_DATA
  ENCRYPTION = (TYPE = 'SNOWFLAKE_SSE') DIRECTORY = (ENABLE = TRUE);
CREATE FILE FORMAT IF NOT EXISTS LAB_CSV
  TYPE = CSV SKIP_HEADER = 1 FIELD_OPTIONALLY_ENCLOSED_BY = '"';

-- 5. Empty tables: rerunning setup does not replace existing rows
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS PATIENTS (
  PATIENT_ID VARCHAR, FIRST_NAME VARCHAR, LAST_NAME VARCHAR, BIRTHDATE DATE,
  GENDER VARCHAR, RACE VARCHAR, CITY VARCHAR, COUNTY VARCHAR, STATE VARCHAR,
  INCOME NUMBER(10,0), PAYER VARCHAR, PRIMARY_CONDITION VARCHAR
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ENCOUNTERS (
  ENCOUNTER_ID VARCHAR, PATIENT_ID VARCHAR, START_TS TIMESTAMP_NTZ, STOP_TS TIMESTAMP_NTZ,
  ENCOUNTER_CLASS VARCHAR, DESCRIPTION VARCHAR, TOTAL_COST NUMBER(12,2), PAYER_COVERAGE NUMBER(12,2)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS CLINICAL_NOTES (
  NOTE_ID VARCHAR, PATIENT_ID VARCHAR, ENCOUNTER_ID VARCHAR,
  NOTE_DATE DATE, NOTE_TYPE VARCHAR, NOTE_TEXT VARCHAR
);

DESCRIBE COMPUTE POOL LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL;
SHOW PARAMETERS LIKE 'DEFAULT_STREAMLIT_COMPUTE_POOL' IN ACCOUNT;
SHOW TABLES IN SCHEMA DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE;
What just happened?You created LAB_WH for SQL queries and LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL for the Python app, plus DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE, a file stage, a CSV format, and three tables. The stage holds files; the tables hold queryable rows.
The pool can stay suspended for nowOn a fresh run, expect SUSPENDED with zero active nodes. It starts automatically when you run the app; first startup can take a few minutes. The two-node maximum leaves room for the private preview and optional deployed app. Its 60-second auto-suspend applies only when no services or jobs are active, not when nobody clicks the app. If the pool already existed, review its settings with the facilitator because IF NOT EXISTS does not update them.

Reference: CREATE COMPUTE POOL and Streamlit default compute pools.

2. Upload CSVs to the database stage, not the workspace

Download lab data (ZIP)

If you already downloaded it, use that copy. Unzip snowcamp-data.zip on your laptop and locate the three CSV files. Upload the extracted CSVs, not the ZIP or its containing folder.

  1. Keep the Snowsight user-menu role at ACCOUNTADMIN. Open Ingestion → Add Data → Load files into a Stage.
  2. Select all three downloaded files: patients.csv, encounters.csv, and clinical_notes.csv. Keep the filenames unchanged.
  3. Select database DAY0_LAB, schema HEALTHCARE, and stage LAB_DATA. Leave the optional path blank so files land at the stage root.
  4. Select Upload and wait for completion. This stores files; it does not load table rows yet.
  5. Return to snowcamp and open data/load_data.sql. Run the context statements and LIST first. Expect exactly the three CSV filenames.

Alternative navigation for viewing files: Catalog → Explorer → DAY0_LAB → HEALTHCARE → Stages → LAB_DATA. See staging files using Snowsight.

3. Load the staged files into tables

Run the rest of data/load_data.sql, or copy this block. Read each COPY result: LOADED, expected row count, and 0 errors.

USE WAREHOUSE LAB_WH;
USE SCHEMA DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE;
LIST @LAB_DATA;

COPY INTO PATIENTS FROM @LAB_DATA
  FILES = ('patients.csv') FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'LAB_CSV')
  ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
COPY INTO ENCOUNTERS FROM @LAB_DATA
  FILES = ('encounters.csv') FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'LAB_CSV')
  ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
COPY INTO CLINICAL_NOTES FROM @LAB_DATA
  FILES = ('clinical_notes.csv') FILE_FORMAT = (FORMAT_NAME = 'LAB_CSV')
  ON_ERROR = 'ABORT_STATEMENT';
Retry without duplicatesCOPY normally skips unchanged files it already loaded. If one upload failed, correct it and rerun load_data.sql; do not add FORCE=TRUE. An already-loaded file being skipped is normal.
If you see this error "Number of columns in file does not match" or "Numeric value 'PATIENT_ID' is not recognized": the header row is being parsed incorrectly. Check that the file is the original CSV and the COPY uses LAB_CSV from setup. It skips the header and handles quoted commas in notes. A missing-file error usually means an altered filename or a nonempty upload path; compare with LIST @LAB_DATA.

Check your work

SELECT 'PATIENTS' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS row_count FROM PATIENTS
UNION ALL SELECT 'ENCOUNTERS', COUNT(*) FROM ENCOUNTERS
UNION ALL SELECT 'CLINICAL_NOTES', COUNT(*) FROM CLINICAL_NOTES;

You should see 500, 5,000 and 1,500.

Recovery only: uploads remain blocked or counts are wrong

Ask the facilitator first. Open data/fallback_data.sql in your Git-connected workspace. If using the manual-upload fallback, download fallback_data.sql and upload it into snowcamp. It replaces all rows in the three lab tables with the exact downloaded dataset; it does not append to partial loads. It must not be used on customized or production tables.

Run setup first, then run the entire recovery file. Its transaction rolls back all three replacements if a load fails; stop and review the error rather than continuing. After success, verify 500 / 5,000 / 1,500 rows and continue to SQL Basics. Do not combine recovery with another CSV load.

SQL Basics

Before you begin: open the prepopulated SQL file

explore.sql is included at the repository root with all the SQL below, in the same numbered order. No copying and pasting is needed.

  1. Open Projects → Workspaces and select your snowcamp workspace.
  2. Open explore.sql. If it is missing from an older workspace, download explore.sql and upload it with + Add new → Upload Files. Preserve any existing personal practice file under a different name before uploading; do not overwrite your own work.
  3. Select and run section 0. Set the context, then run sections 1-6 one at a time. Use the selected-statement Run control rather than Run all, and inspect each result. Section 6 creates the view needed by the app.

Each SQL file can have a different context, so run section 0 even if you already ran setup in another file. Keep ACCOUNTADMIN selected. The code below is a reading reference; run the matching section already in explore.sql. You can add your own practice at the bottom; no Git commit or push is needed.

USE WAREHOUSE LAB_WH;
USE SCHEMA DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE;

1. Look at some rows

SELECT * FROM PATIENTS LIMIT 10;

* means "every column". LIMIT keeps the result small. Use it whenever you're exploring a table.

2. Filter and sort

SELECT FIRST_NAME, LAST_NAME, CITY, PAYER
FROM PATIENTS
WHERE CITY = 'Boston'
  AND PAYER = 'Medicare'
ORDER BY LAST_NAME;
Watch outText inside quotes is case-sensitive: 'boston' won't match 'Boston'. Unquoted column and table names are case-insensitive; double-quoted identifiers preserve case.

3. Count and total with GROUP BY

SELECT ENCOUNTER_CLASS,
       COUNT(*)                  AS encounters,
       ROUND(AVG(TOTAL_COST), 2) AS avg_cost,
       SUM(TOTAL_COST)           AS total_cost
FROM ENCOUNTERS
GROUP BY ENCOUNTER_CLASS
ORDER BY total_cost DESC;

Which kind of visit costs the most in total? Inpatient visits are rare but expensive.

Read the resultThe first row has the highest TOTAL_COST. Compare its encounter count with the other rows: does the most frequent visit type also cost the most in total? You will chart this breakdown in the Streamlit module.

4. Combine tables with JOIN

Encounters only store a PATIENT_ID. To see costs by city or insurer, you join to PATIENTS:

SELECT p.PAYER,
       COUNT(*)                                  AS encounters,
       SUM(e.TOTAL_COST)                         AS total_cost,
       SUM(e.TOTAL_COST - e.PAYER_COVERAGE)      AS patient_out_of_pocket
FROM ENCOUNTERS e
JOIN PATIENTS p ON p.PATIENT_ID = e.PATIENT_ID
GROUP BY p.PAYER
ORDER BY patient_out_of_pocket DESC;

e and p are short nicknames (aliases) for the tables.

5. Work with dates

SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', START_TS) AS month,
       COUNT(*)                     AS encounters
FROM ENCOUNTERS
WHERE ENCOUNTER_CLASS = 'emergency'
GROUP BY month
ORDER BY month;

Read the results in month order. Find a month with more emergency visits than the previous month. This exercise uses the result table; no chart control is required.

6. Save a query as a view

A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. Your app in the Streamlit section will read from this view.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY AS
SELECT e.ENCOUNTER_ID,
       e.PATIENT_ID,
       p.CITY,
       p.PAYER,
       DATEDIFF('year', p.BIRTHDATE, e.START_TS::DATE)
         - IFF(DATEADD('year', DATEDIFF('year', p.BIRTHDATE, e.START_TS::DATE),
                       p.BIRTHDATE) > e.START_TS::DATE, 1, 0) AS AGE_AT_VISIT,
       e.ENCOUNTER_CLASS,
       e.START_TS::DATE                          AS VISIT_DATE,
       e.TOTAL_COST,
       e.PAYER_COVERAGE,
       e.TOTAL_COST - e.PAYER_COVERAGE           AS OUT_OF_POCKET
FROM ENCOUNTERS e
JOIN PATIENTS p ON p.PATIENT_ID = e.PATIENT_ID;

SELECT * FROM ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY LIMIT 10;

7. Peek under the hood

Go to Monitoring › Query History and click one of your queries. Open the Query Profile tab to see each step Snowflake took and how long it took. When a query is slow, this is the first place to look.

Try it with CoCo

Time Travel: Undo Your Mistakes

Open the supplied time_travel.ipynb notebook. It contains the explanations, SQL cells, and recovery checkpoints; no code needs to be copied from this page. Snowflake keeps historical data within the table's retention period, normally one day for these lab tables.

1. Open and connect the notebook

  1. In Projects → Workspaces → snowcamp, open time_travel.ipynb at the workspace root. If missing, download the Time Travel notebook and upload it with + Add new → Upload Files.
  2. Confirm the notebook picker shows ACCOUNTADMIN and select LAB_WH as its query warehouse. If the role is different, ask the facilitator to correct the initial setup.
  3. Connect to the facilitator-approved CPU notebook service/pool. Use a short idle timeout, such as 15 minutes if offered. Notebook compute is separate from the SQL warehouse; the facilitator must verify NOTEBOOK workloads are allowed. Do not assume the Streamlit pool's configuration is suitable or create extra pools to bypass a restriction.
  4. Use Run this cell only (Cmd+Enter on Mac, Ctrl+Enter on Windows) for each SQL cell. The SQL and fully qualified table names are already present.
Do not use Run allThe notebook intentionally changes data, drops a table, and demonstrates an error. Run each cell separately and read its checkpoint. Keep the same notebook session through restoration; do not restart or suspend compute halfway through.

2. Follow the notebook sections

  1. Check the starting data: verify 500 patients, 5,000 encounters, and 1,500 notes. Save the original ten-city counts outside the notebook output.
  2. Create the safety copy: run the first-run clone cell. If PATIENTS_BEFORE_EXERCISE already exists, stop before the UPDATE. Do not rename, replace, or drop it. Have the facilitator verify the clone and follow the notebook's rerun instructions.
  3. Save the time, then make a mistake: run the timestamp cell before the UPDATE. The next result shows all 500 patients in Boston.
  4. Look at the past and restore: query the saved timestamp, restore the rows, and compare the city counts with the original.
  5. Bring back a dropped table: run DROP, then the separate SELECT cell. That SELECT should fail. Run the UNDROP cell directly afterward, not Run all above, and confirm 1,500 notes again.
CheckpointThe original city counts are restored and DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.CLINICAL_NOTES has 1,500 rows. Complete both checks before moving on. The sandbox clone is optional; skip the notebook's recovery-only cells on the normal path.
If the timestamp is lostDo not capture a new timestamp after the mistake. The notebook includes a recovery-only section using the verified original safety clone. If the clone is missing or uncertain, stop and ask the facilitator. The separate exact-data fallback resets all three lab tables.

3. Suspend notebook compute after recovery

After both tables are restored, open Connected, hover over your notebook service, and select Suspend (pause icon). This clears session variables. Closing a browser tab alone does not stop notebook compute. Then continue to Streamlit. Export results as HTML if you want to keep them; outputs are not stored in the notebook file.

Your First Streamlit App

Streamlit turns a short Python script into an interactive web app. In Snowflake, the app runs right next to your data, so there are no servers, passwords or files to move.

1. Create the app inside your workspace

  1. Open Projects → Workspaces → snowcamp. Leave ACCOUNTADMIN selected for the entire exercise.
  2. Select + Add new → Streamlit app. Snowflake creates an app folder with streamlit_app.py, pyproject.toml, snowflake.yml, and .streamlit/config.toml. Use the newly created folder for your app, not the repository's reference streamlit folder.
  3. Open the generated streamlit_app.py. In the app's Settings → Execution, select LAB_WH as the query warehouse. Setup configured LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL as the account's default compute pool. The app runs on a container runtime; the warehouse runs its SQL queries.
  4. Select Run to preview the starter app. This is your private development app; no database or schema selection is needed until deployment.
Before this moduleComplete setup, including creation of LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL, its default-pool setting, and your LAB_WH default warehouse. The facilitator must verify Streamlit workloads are allowed and the pool can start in the workshop region. If the Streamlit option is missing or the preview cannot start, stop and ask the facilitator; do not switch roles or create extra compute pools to work around it.
Two kinds of computeLAB_STREAMLIT_POOL runs Python; LAB_WH runs database queries. Both can incur charges. The warehouse's 60-second auto-suspend does not stop the compute pool, and a running app keeps its pool active. Workspace compute nodes are released after three hours of inactivity; follow the pool-suspension step in Wrap-Up when finished.

2. Replace the starter code

Inside the new app folder, replace the sample in streamlit_app.py with the code below, then select Run. Keep the generated configuration files; do not paste Python into them.

The repository's streamlit/streamlit_app.py is a completed reference copy, including notes search. For this exercise, build incrementally with the two blocks below. Use the runtime's pre-installed packages; do not add or pin dependencies for this lab.

import streamlit as st

st.title("Encounter Explorer")
st.caption("Synthetic teaching data | DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY")

conn = st.connection("snowflake")  # Snowflake supplies the credentials

# Cache the view for 60 seconds, then apply sidebar filters locally.
df = conn.query("SELECT * FROM DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY", ttl=60)

# Sidebar filters
cities = st.sidebar.multiselect("City", sorted(df["CITY"].unique()))
payers = st.sidebar.multiselect("Payer", sorted(df["PAYER"].unique()))
if cities:
    df = df[df["CITY"].isin(cities)]
if payers:
    df = df[df["PAYER"].isin(payers)]

# Headline numbers
c1, c2, c3 = st.columns(3)
c1.metric("Encounters", f"{len(df):,}")
c2.metric("Patients", f"{df['PATIENT_ID'].nunique():,}")
c3.metric("Total cost", f"${df['TOTAL_COST'].sum():,.0f}")

st.subheader("Total cost by encounter class")
st.bar_chart(df.groupby("ENCOUNTER_CLASS")["TOTAL_COST"].sum())

st.subheader("Most expensive encounters")
st.dataframe(df.sort_values("TOTAL_COST", ascending=False).head(20), width="stretch")

3. Play with it

  • Pick a city or two in the sidebar. The numbers and the chart update right away.
  • Try a change yourself: replace "ENCOUNTER_CLASS" in the bar_chart line with "PAYER", then click Run.

4. Add a clinical notes search

Paste this at the bottom of your code and click Run:

st.subheader("Search clinical notes")
term = st.text_input("Find notes containing", "shortness of breath")
if term:
    notes = conn.query(
        """SELECT NOTE_DATE, PATIENT_ID, NOTE_TEXT
           FROM DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.CLINICAL_NOTES
           WHERE NOTE_TEXT ILIKE ?
           ORDER BY NOTE_DATE DESC
           LIMIT 50""",
        params=[f"%{term}%"],
        ttl=60,
    )
    st.write(f"Showing {len(notes)} matching notes (maximum 50; not a total count)")
    st.dataframe(notes, width="stretch")

Type different words, such as fatigue or refer to specialist. Submit the text input with Enter to rerun the script with the new value.

Good habitThe ? and params= pass the user's text to Snowflake as a value, not as part of the SQL. That stops someone from typing something that changes your query. Never paste user input straight into a SQL string.
How this worksst.connection("snowflake") uses the platform-provided connection; no password or secrets file is needed. Queries use fully qualified object names and cache results for 60 seconds. The development preview is private. If deployed with the default owner's-rights model, the app uses its owner role (ACCOUNTADMIN in this isolated lab), not each viewer's table privileges. Use a dedicated least-privilege owner role in production.

5. Preview now; deploy only if needed

The core lab is complete with the private workspace preview. Run previews your edits; it does not publish them. There is no need to commit or push to Git.

Optional: deploy a Streamlit object from the workspace
  1. Select Deploy in the app's project pane. Set the app title to Encounter Explorer and the location to DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.
  2. Confirm LAB_STREAMLIT_POOL as the compute pool and LAB_WH as the query warehouse. The pool allows up to two nodes for the preview and deployed app. Do not add external access integrations or additional sharing roles for this lab. Leave ACCOUNTADMIN as the owner role.
  3. Select Deploy. This creates the deployed Streamlit object; it is separate from your development preview. Access follows the object's grants.
  4. After future code edits, use Run to check them privately, then Deploy again only when you want to update the deployed app. Editing workspace code alone does not update that app.

Reference: Create and run a Streamlit app in a workspace.

Glossary

SnowsightThe Snowflake web interface
Virtual warehouseCompute that runs your queries. It's billed in credits while running and stores no data.
CreditThe unit Snowflake uses to bill compute. Rates vary by service, warehouse type and generation.
Database / schemaContainers that organize tables and views
RoleA named set of permissions; a session has one primary role and can activate secondary roles.
ViewA saved query you can select from like a table
Time TravelQuerying or restoring earlier versions of your data
Zero-copy cloneAn instant copy that shares storage with the original until either one changes
StreamlitA Python framework for data apps, which runs inside Snowflake

The pool is configured to auto-resume when used again, so reopening an app can restart it. Suspending LAB_WH alone does not suspend the pool. Your warehouse also pauses after 60 idle seconds; if it is still running, you can pause it now:

SQL Challenges

Now it's your turn. Try each question on your own first, then click Show answer to compare. There's usually more than one correct way to write it.

1. How many patients are in each city?

Hint: GROUP BY, like the encounter query in SQL Basics.

Show answer 
SELECT CITY, COUNT(*) AS patients
FROM PATIENTS
GROUP BY CITY
ORDER BY patients DESC;

2. Which 5 patients had the most emergency visits?

Hint: join ENCOUNTERS to PATIENTS, filter with WHERE, and finish with LIMIT 5.

Show answer 
SELECT p.PATIENT_ID, p.FIRST_NAME, p.LAST_NAME, COUNT(*) AS er_visits
FROM ENCOUNTERS e
JOIN PATIENTS p ON p.PATIENT_ID = e.PATIENT_ID
WHERE e.ENCOUNTER_CLASS = 'emergency'
GROUP BY p.PATIENT_ID, p.FIRST_NAME, p.LAST_NAME
ORDER BY er_visits DESC, p.PATIENT_ID
LIMIT 5;

3. What is the average cost per visit for each primary condition?

Hint: PRIMARY_CONDITION is on PATIENTS, and costs are on ENCOUNTERS.

Show answer 
SELECT p.PRIMARY_CONDITION,
       COUNT(*)                    AS encounters,
       ROUND(AVG(e.TOTAL_COST), 2) AS avg_cost
FROM ENCOUNTERS e
JOIN PATIENTS p ON p.PATIENT_ID = e.PATIENT_ID
GROUP BY p.PRIMARY_CONDITION
ORDER BY avg_cost DESC;

4. Which payers cover patients aged 65 and over?

Hint: the ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY view already has an AGE_AT_VISIT column. To count unique patients, use COUNT(DISTINCT ...).

Show answer 
SELECT PAYER, COUNT(DISTINCT PATIENT_ID) AS patients_65_plus
FROM ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY
WHERE AGE_AT_VISIT >= 65
GROUP BY PAYER
ORDER BY patients_65_plus DESC;

5. How many clinical notes mention "shortness of breath"?

Hint: ILIKE searches text without caring about upper or lower case. % means "anything".

Show answer 
SELECT COUNT(*) AS notes
FROM CLINICAL_NOTES
WHERE NOTE_TEXT ILIKE '%shortness of breath%';
Why this mattersChallenge 5 searches for exact words. In the Cortex AI Lab, Cortex Search finds notes by meaning instead, so a search for "trouble breathing" can find "shortness of breath".

Roles and Access

Optional extension (10 minutes).Finish the core lab first. The care team should query the encounter view, but not patient names or birthdates. Stay on ACCOUNTADMIN. Open a separate access.sql file to keep these examples organized; this exercise creates and inspects grants without changing your active role.

1. Create a care-team role

CREATE ROLE IF NOT EXISTS CARE_TEAM;
GRANT ROLE CARE_TEAM TO ROLE ACCOUNTADMIN;

This places the teaching role under the lab administrator. It does not activate CARE_TEAM or change your session role.

2. Grant only what's needed

GRANT USAGE  ON WAREHOUSE LAB_WH                        TO ROLE CARE_TEAM;
GRANT USAGE  ON DATABASE  DAY0_LAB                      TO ROLE CARE_TEAM;
GRANT USAGE  ON SCHEMA    DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE           TO ROLE CARE_TEAM;
GRANT SELECT ON VIEW      DAY0_LAB.HEALTHCARE.ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY TO ROLE CARE_TEAM;
Why so many grants?To read a view, a role needs access at every level: the warehouse to run the query, plus the database, the schema and the view itself. These statements grant no direct access to PATIENTS or CLINICAL_NOTES. The view excludes names and birthdates, but includes identifiers and encounter details; it is not anonymized.

3. Inspect the grants without switching roles

SHOW GRANTS TO ROLE CARE_TEAM;
SHOW GRANTS OF ROLE CARE_TEAM;
SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();

In the first result, find the warehouse, database and schema USAGE grants and the SELECT grant on ENCOUNTER_SUMMARY. The second shows that CARE_TEAM was granted to ACCOUNTADMIN. The final result should still be ACCOUNTADMIN.

Inspecting is not an access-denial testQueries you run as ACCOUNTADMIN use administrator privileges, not just the grants on CARE_TEAM. We do not run permission-denial tests in this single-role lab. Existing grants, inherited roles, and PUBLIC privileges can affect effective access; review unexpected grants with the facilitator.

4. Review sharing before granting app access

  1. Leave ACCOUNTADMIN selected. If you deployed the optional Streamlit object, open Projects → Streamlit → Encounter Explorer → Share to inspect its controls without adding recipients. If you only ran the workspace preview, keep it private and review the following scenario instead; deployment is not required.
  2. The app includes individual encounters and clinical notes. A role that can only query the summary view directly could still see notes through this owner-rights app. Keep it private unless the intended audience is authorized for every displayed field.
Good to knowA deployed app using the default owner's-rights connection runs with its owner's permissions, which for this lab is ACCOUNTADMIN. Anyone you share it with can see the app's displayed data even without direct table grants. Use a dedicated least-privilege owner role for production apps. The files in this lab are synthetic, but the same sharing decision matters for real data.
